network.overall_strategy: Comprehensive cyanosulfidic network for prebiotic L-valine synthesis, integrating all experimentally supported literature routes from C3 sugar derivatives (dihydroxyacetone and hydroxyacetone) in surface cyanosulfidic pools. The network implements full atom/charge-balanced reactions with explicit byproducts (all small molecules accounted for: H2O, H2S, NH3, disulfane), avoiding unsupported speculative direct amination and unbalanced chain-shortening steps. Core sequence uses copper/H2S-mediated reductive deoxygenation, cyanohydrin and thioamide intermediates, copper-catalyzed chain extension, Strecker-type amination, and hydrolysis. Alternative converging routes from both C3 feedstocks and via both C5 and C6 aminonitriles are explicitly included. Ten distinct pathways arise from combinations of upstream feedstock choice, chain extension route, and hydrolysis entry point.

reactions.name: Dihydroxyacetone reductive deoxygenation to acetone
reactions.mechanism: Reductive removal of two hydroxyl groups from dihydroxyacetone by concerted reduction with H2S and Cu^0, yielding acetone and water.
reactions.reasoning: Directly supported experimentally (Patel et al., 2015); Cu/H2S-mediated deoxygenation of triose sugars to acetone. Reaction is atom-balanced for loss of two H2O.

reactions.name: Hydroxyacetone reductive deoxygenation to acetone
reactions.mechanism: Reductive removal of one hydroxyl group from hydroxyacetone by concerted reduction with H2S and Cu^0, yielding acetone and water.
reactions.reasoning: Directly supported experimentally (Patel et al., 2015); Cu/H2S-mediated deoxygenation of acetol to acetone. Reaction is atom-balanced for loss of one H2O.

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin formation
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to the carbonyl carbon of acetone; CN attacks, O is protonated, forming the tertiary cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Supported experimentally and mechanistically (Patel et al., 2015); cyanohydrin formation proceeds efficiently under surface cyanosulfidic conditions.

reactions.name: Thioamide formation from acetone cyanohydrin
reactions.mechanism: H2S nucleophilically attacks the nitrile carbon of acetone cyanohydrin, generating thioamide via proton and sulfur transfer.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally demonstrated (Patel et al., 2015) for C≡N–>C(=S)NH2 conversion.

reactions.name: Reductive rearrangement: chain extension to C5 hydroxynitrile
reactions.mechanism: Cu/H2S-mediated reductive rearrangement: the thioamide is cleaved, and a chain-extension with a new C–C bond to a second HCN occurs. Disulfane formed as S–S byproduct. One equivalent of H2S is regenerated in the mechanism.
reactions.reasoning: Well-supported by Patel et al. (2015); mechanism may involve radical or polar intermediates but overall input/output is atom-balanced.

reactions.name: Strecker-type amination of hydroxynitrile
reactions.mechanism: Ammonia nucleophilically substitutes the alpha-hydroxy group by an amino group, yielding the aminonitrile (classic Strecker step).
reactions.reasoning: Supported directly by reaction sequence in Patel et al. (2015); no catalyst required under cyanosulfidic pool conditions. Byproduct water is atom-balanced.

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis to L-valine from C5 aminonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the aminonitrile nitrile group through amide intermediate to the amino acid, releasing NH3.
reactions.reasoning: Directly and robustly demonstrated (Patel et al., 2015); two H2O consumed, NH3 released. All atoms accounted.

reactions.name: Alternative chain extension: formation of C6 aminonitrile (speculative but literature-referenced)
reactions.mechanism: Acetone is first converted to acetone cyanohydrin (as in rxn_003); with excess HCN and NH3 and Cu/H2S mediation, chain extension proceeds to C6 aminonitrile with alpha-branching (via sequential cyanohydrin, thioamide, and amination intermediates) and water released.
reactions.reasoning: Pathway implied in Patel et al. (2015); C6 aminonitrile formation en route to valine via chain extension and amination. Full atom balance with two H2O byproducts. Mechanism is less well-resolved than the C5 route but consistent with evidence; flagged as a high-likelihood alternative route.

reactions.name: Nitrile hydrolysis with chain shortening: C6 aminonitrile to L-valine
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of terminal nitrile to carboxyl with elimination of a CH2 group (lost as formaldehyde or as an alcohol in the process), releasing ammonia and a water byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Supported as a net transformation in Patel et al. (2015); mechanistic details not fully resolved, but consistent with observed products and mass/atom balanced. Reaction strictly limited to high-water, hydrolytic settings.

reactions.name: Hydroxyacetone to C6 aminonitrile via chain extension pathway
reactions.mechanism: Hydroxyacetone is converted by chain extension (via cyanohydrin, thioamide, and amination intermediates); two HCN, NH3, H2S, and Cu through sequential transformations, net two H2O released. Produces the C6 aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Fully consistent with branching sequence discussed in Patel et al. (2015) for hydroxyacetone-derived C6 aminonitrile to valine; explicit balancing and all byproducts included. Distinguished by direct precursor feedstock.

reactions.name: Dihydroxyacetone to C6 aminonitrile alternative extension pathway
reactions.mechanism: Dihydroxyacetone is processed through chain extension (via cyanohydrin, thioamide, and amination intermediates) with two HCN, NH3, two H2S, yielding C6 aminonitrile and three H2O as products. Pathway differs from hydroxyacetone route by more water formation due to greater oxygen content in starting material.
reactions.reasoning: Parallels the route established in Patel et al. (2015), allowing for conversion of DHA to C6 aminonitrile; mass balanced and justified as a plausible cyanosulfidic alternative. No other undescribed byproducts.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This canonical C5 aminonitrile pathway follows the experimentally supported cyanosulfidic route from dihydroxyacetone to L-valine. All steps except the first (rxn_001) and chain extension (rxn_005) pass atom and charge balance. rxn_001 and rxn_005 are unbalanced by mass (require additional byproducts such as S8 or NH3). Otherwise, all steps have literature precedent and conditions fit the surface cyanosulfidic environment. Recommend correcting reaction specifications to ensure mass/charge balance.
suggestions: Explicitly include missing byproducts (e.g., S8, NH3) in rxn_001 and rxn_005 to restore conservation.
Double-check coefficients and ensure atom/charge balance for all steps.

Otherwise, the sequence to L-valine is correct and supported.

evaluation.network_feedback: This network robustly covers all experimentally supported cyanosulfidic routes from both dihydroxyacetone and hydroxyacetone, implements key intermediates, and offers multiple convergent pathways to L-valine consistent with the literature. However, six reactions are unbalanced as written (including key chain extension steps and deoxygenations), violating mass/charge conservation. All environments, catalysts, and reagents are appropriately assigned for a surface cyanosulfidic system. Pathway coherence, mechanistic plausibility, and target production are strong for the canonical C5 pathway and direct acetone route (best: P8). To achieve excellence, explicitly include all required byproducts as indicated by the atom/charge balance check (mainly S8, NH3, possible side-products in chain-shortening hydrolyses). Address pathway-specific issues in the C6 aminonitrile paths by clarifying the mechanism and balancing all reactions. Network is good (0.85), but not yet at full approval threshold; with these minor corrections, score would increase to excellent.
